title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2026
key_claim: Joint BoE/FCA survey of 196 firms: 86% use AI (75% in 2024); the top three model/API providers account for 54% of reported relationships (55% on the Chart 9 measure, up from 41% in 2024) against 79% for the top three cloud/compute providers; third-party implementations are 53% of highly material AI systems (35% in 2024); only 24% have deep knowledge of third-party AI systems; 81% rely on vendor assurance and contracts; concern about critical third-party dependencies rated high or severe rises from 40% today to 63% in one to three years; only 14% of 226 model API/hosting relationships are both high criticality and hard to substitute, against 37% of 169 cloud relationships.
frame_summary: The supervisors' own data show UK finance becoming dependent on a few external AI model and cloud providers with limited visibility into those systems, though the model layer is still more substitutable than cloud.

title: UK financial system strengthened with new safeguards for major technology providers
key_claim: HM Treasury designated four cloud and technology providers as Critical Third Parties from 13 July 2026 (Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited, Google Cloud EMEA Limited, Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, Oracle Corporation UK Limited), overseen by the Bank of England, PRA and FCA. The release does not mention AI or any AI model provider.
frame_summary: The government presents the first Critical Third Party designations as closing the systemic-supplier gap, framed entirely around cloud services.

title: Digital innovation: hindrance or booster for banks’ business models?
key_claim: ECB Supervisory Board Chair Claudia Buch: around two-thirds of euro area banks have cooperation agreements with external providers, often outside the EU, often in highly concentrated markets with limited substitutability; more than 90% of directly supervised banks integrate AI.
frame_summary: The ECB's top supervisor argues AI adoption is near-universal among euro area banks and presents reliance on a few concentrated, mostly non-EU providers as a dependency risk supervisors must see across the system.

title: FSB finalises sound practices for the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)
key_claim: The FSB's final report sets out 12 sound practices, including (xii) management of risks from third-party AI dependencies, and strongly encourages boards and senior management of financial institutions to reference them.
frame_summary: The global standard-setter puts third-party AI dependency on the board's own agenda as a firm-level governance practice rather than proposing direct oversight of model providers.

title: When machines attack: frontier AI cyber threats and policy responses in the financial sector
key_claim: FSI Occasional Paper No 28: reliance on common cloud, software and frontier AI providers creates concentration and sovereign access risks, where one provider's disruption or policy decision can cascade across firms and jurisdictions; policy responses so far reinforce existing cyber and operational-resilience rules rather than creating AI-specific regimes.
frame_summary: Argues frontier AI providers are a new single point of failure whose risk includes access and policy decisions, not only outages, while authorities are responding through existing rules.
verbatim_quote: Reliance on common cloud, software and frontier AI providers introduces concentration and sovereign access risks, whereby a single provider's disruption or policy decision can cascade across firms and jurisdictions.

title: Global Financial Markets Face Rising Risks From AI, Bond Yields, and Cyberattacks
key_claim: October 2026 GFSR blog: frontier AI models could accelerate attacks and defences, raising the importance of oversight of critical third-party providers; in more than 70% of reported cases this year software providers had almost no time to patch before exploitation.
frame_summary: The IMF frames AI as a twin financial-stability risk, valuation and leverage on one side and cyber and common-provider contagion on the other, and calls for stronger critical third-party oversight.
verbatim_quote: Frontier AI models could accelerate both attacks and defenses, increasing the importance of cyber resilience, incident reporting, crisis preparedness, and oversight of critical third-party providers.

title: Key lessons from the Bank of England and FCA's 2026 survey
key_claim: Professional analysis of the BoE/FCA survey: third-party AI services are the most important finding for lawyers and risk professionals; contract priorities are audit rights, change management for model updates and liability allocation; only 2% deploy agents with broad autonomy.
frame_summary: Argues model-layer dependence is now a contractual and governance problem firms must solve themselves, through audit rights, change control on model updates and liability terms.
verbatim_quote: One of the most important findings for lawyers and risk professionals relates to third-party AI services.
notes: Authors Wendy Saunders and Helen Hart. Supports the bottom-up via contracts mechanism. title: Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, sources say
key_claim: Six sources say bank regulators are stepping up AI scrutiny; euro zone banks are being asked to map AI use across their businesses and third-party providers; the ECB set an end-October deadline in a July letter for plans against AI-enabled cyber threats; regulators are gathering information rather than writing rules.
frame_summary: Reuters reports supervisors moving from watching to information-gathering, starting by mapping banks' AI and third-party provider dependencies rather than writing new rules.
